dimred.q: What does PCA's first principal component represent?
options: The original column with the largest values
The direction through the data with the most variance
The cluster that contains the most points
The column most correlated with the target
dimred.why: PC1 is a new axis, a weighted mix of columns, along which the data spreads the most. It is not chosen using the target.

dimred.q: In the curse of dimensionality, what happens to distances as you add many columns?
options: Nearest and farthest neighbours end up at almost the same distance
All distances shrink towards zero so every point looks identical
Distances become exact, so k-nearest neighbours improves
Distances stay the same but training becomes slower
dimred.why: In high dimensions the ratio of farthest to nearest distance approaches 1, so 'nearest' carries little information.

dimred.q: Hollin Logistics (a client) has 120 sensor columns in kilograms, degrees and percent. Before PCA, what do you do first?
options: Drop every column measured in percent
Run PCA on the raw columns to keep the original units
Standardise the columns so each has mean 0 and sd 1
Sort the columns by their average value
dimred.why: PCA follows variance, so columns with large units would dominate. Standardising puts them on an equal footing.

dimred.q: A product lead at Marrowby Media shows a t-SNE plot of article embeddings with 6 blobs and says 'we have 6 audiences'. Best reply?
options: Agree, since t-SNE preserves the true number of groups
Measure blob sizes on the plot to size each audience
Rerun with a lower perplexity to confirm there are exactly 6
Treat it as a hint and test groups with clustering on the original data
dimred.why: Blob counts and sizes change with settings. Clustering on the original or PCA-reduced data, plus reading samples, tests the idea properly.

dimred.q: Spot the mistake: 'We fitted PCA on all 10,000 rows, then split into train and test and trained the model.'
options: PCA must always keep 95 percent of variance
PCA saw the test rows, so information leaked into the features
PCA should be fitted on the test set only
The model should have been trained before PCA
dimred.why: Fitting PCA before the split lets test data shape the components. Put PCA in a Pipeline fitted on training rows only.

options: A value that is extreme compared with all other values
A value that is normal in one setting but odd in another, like 3am
A group of points that are only odd when seen together
A value that is missing from the dataset
anomaly.why: Contextual anomalies depend on context such as time of day. Extreme-for-everyone is a point anomaly; odd-together is collective.

anomaly.q: How does an isolation forest decide a point is unusual?
options: It sits far from the nearest cluster centre
It has a z-score above 3 in any column
Random splits isolate it after only a few steps
A labelled fraud case looks similar to it
anomaly.why: Anomalies are few and different, so random trees separate them quickly. A short average path means a higher anomaly score.

anomaly.q: Tamsford Energy's on-call team can handle about 20 alerts a day. How should you set the alert threshold?
options: Alert on the top 20 scores a day and track precision at 20
Use z greater than 3 because it is the standard rule
Alert on everything and let the team filter manually
Set contamination to 50 percent to be safe
anomaly.why: The review budget sets k. Then precision at k tells you how many alerts are worth the team's time.

anomaly.q: Hourly logins at Quellbrook Software follow a strong daily cycle. Which detector will catch a night-time burst best?
options: A global z-score over all hours
An IQR fence on all hourly values together
A one-class SVM trained on the daily totals
Scoring each hour against the same hour's recent median
anomaly.why: A same-hour baseline removes the daily cycle, so an unusual 3am value stands out. Global methods see it as a normal midday number.

anomaly.q: Spot the trap: refunds of 95 and 60 in a series around 14; only 95 is flagged by |z| > 3. Why was 60 missed?
options: 60 is inside the normal range of the data
The z-score formula ignores values below 100
The 95 inflated the mean and sd, masking the 60
IQR fences were used instead of z-scores
anomaly.why: This is masking. Robust methods such as IQR fences flag both, because percentiles barely move when outliers appear.

timeseries.q: What does a seasonal-naive forecast predict for next Monday with daily data?
options: The average of all past Mondays
The value from last Monday
The value from yesterday
A straight-line trend to next Monday
timeseries.why: Seasonal naive repeats the value from one season ago; with a weekly season that is the same weekday last week.

timeseries.q: In simple exponential smoothing, what does a higher alpha do?
options: Gives more weight to old values, making the forecast smoother
Adds a weekly seasonal term to the forecast
Reacts faster to recent values, making the forecast jumpier
Removes the trend before forecasting
timeseries.why: New level = alpha x latest + (1 - alpha) x old level, so a large alpha follows the latest values closely.

timeseries.q: Harlow Crest Hotels wants room demand 14 days ahead. Which lag feature is safe for a boosting model?
options: Demand from yesterday
Demand from 3 days ago
The 7-day rolling mean ending yesterday
Demand from 14 days before the target day
timeseries.why: When forecasting 14 days ahead, only values at least 14 days before the target day are known at forecast time.

timeseries.q: A client says their new model has 3% MAPE. What do you ask first?
options: Was the test split by time, and what does seasonal naive score?
Which neural network architecture did you use?
Can we switch the metric to R-squared instead?
How many features does the model use?
timeseries.why: A shuffled split leaks the future, and a number means little without the baseline scored on the same test.

timeseries.q: Spot the trap: a slow-selling product has some zero-sales days. Which metric breaks?
options: MAE, because it cannot handle zeros
WAPE, because it divides by each day's value
MAPE, because dividing by a zero actual is undefined
MASE, because it needs a seasonal baseline
timeseries.why: MAPE divides each error by the actual value, so a zero makes it infinite. WAPE divides by the total, which is fine.

options: Recommending items with similar descriptions to ones the user liked
Recommending from patterns in many users' behaviour
Letting users vote on which items to feature
Filtering out items that are out of stock
recsys.why: CF learns 'people who bought this also bought that' from behaviour. Similar descriptions is content-based filtering.

recsys.q: Why does NDCG@k add information that precision@k lacks?
options: It counts how many items are in the catalogue
It measures revenue instead of clicks
It rewards relevant items more when they appear near the top
It only works with star ratings
recsys.why: Precision@k ignores order inside the top k. NDCG discounts hits lower in the list, matching how people scan.

recsys.q: Pellbrook Books adds 400 new titles a month with no sales yet. How do you get them recommended?
options: Wait until collaborative filtering picks them up
Show them only to users who rated many books
Remove them from the catalogue until they sell
Use content similarity and reserve some slots for new titles
recsys.why: New items have no behaviour, so CF cannot score them. Content similarity plus guaranteed exposure solves cold start.

recsys.q: Ostwick Home has only views and purchases. Offline, a new model beats bestsellers on NDCG. What next?
options: Run an A/B test with a primary metric and guardrails
Ship it to everyone since offline metrics prove value
Retrain on star ratings before deciding
Replace NDCG with accuracy and re-evaluate
recsys.why: Offline metrics pick candidates, but only a live A/B test on a business metric shows real impact.

recsys.q: Spot the mistake: 'We treat every item a user never clicked as a dislike when training.'
options: Clicks should be ignored entirely in recommenders
Most unclicked items were never shown, so they are not dislikes
Dislikes should be weighted more heavily than purchases
Unclicked items should be removed from the catalogue
recsys.why: With implicit feedback, a missing interaction usually means 'not seen', not 'not wanted'.
